Your agent ran all night and wrote 30,000 lines of code. Every check passed. The app was broken. The loop didn't fail — your system did, because nothing in it could stop and ask if you were still solving the right problem. You already did the smart thing and split one agent into a team: a planner, a builder, a reviewer. That's the graph. But connecting agents isn't the same as putting someone in charge. The fix isn't a smarter model — it's a governance layer, an operating system for your agents. And the part you can build today is simple: every decision in your system has exactly one owner.

→ Countable things belong to CODE — budget limits, retry counts, valid JSON, tests passing; never ask a model to check what an IF statement can
→ Ambiguous things belong to the MODEL — why did this fail, the plan or the reviewer; let it diagnose, never let it decide alone
→ The mission belongs to YOU — not an approve button, the one person who owns what "done" actually means
→ That overnight disaster didn't need more intelligence; it needed code to stop the bleeding, a model to say why, and a human holding the goal
→ You already built half an operating system by accident — checkpoints, retries, permissions; the other half you build on purpose
→ A graph connects your agents. An operating system runs them.

Xnj5ta_JxLE.description:
Landing on Mars isn't science fiction anymore, it's something we've done repeatedly with robotic missions since 1976, though no human has made the trip yet.

Scientists believe Mars once closely resembled early Earth. Orbital and rover imagery has revealed ancient river channels, dried lakebeds, and geological evidence consistent with a past ocean covering parts of the northern hemisphere. Over billions of years, Mars lost most of its atmosphere and surface water, leaving behind the dry, iron-oxide-covered world we see today, the source of its distinctive red colour.

Mars is home to Olympus Mons, the largest known volcano in the solar system, standing approximately 21.9 kilometres tall, about two and a half times the height of Mount Everest, with a base roughly the size of Arizona. Nearby lies Valles Marineris, a canyon system stretching over 4,000 kilometres in length and reaching depths of up to 7 kilometres, more than ten times longer and several times deeper than Earth's Grand Canyon.

Average surface temperature sits around minus 63 degrees Celsius, dropping to as low as minus 140 at the poles during winter.

Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, both thought to be captured asteroids. Phobos is gradually spiraling inward due to tidal forces and is expected to either collide with Mars or break apart into a ring system within the next 30 to 50 million years.

One of the most actively studied Martian mysteries involves methane detected by NASA's Curiosity rover, which fluctuates seasonally in ways not yet fully explained. Researchers have not determined whether the source is geological activity or, potentially, biological processes, making it a key focus in the ongoing search for evidence of life.

A Martian day, called a sol, lasts approximately 24 hours and 37 minutes, remarkably close to an Earth day.

Source: NASA, Mars Facts and Exploration. NASA Curiosity Rover, Methane Detection Studies. Wikipedia, Olympus Mons and Valles Marineris.

3yL7rYKYSvY.description:
Welcome to Unknown Worlds, where every episode we take you to a real planet that might just be able to hold life.
TRAPPIST-1 is a red dwarf star system located about 40 light-years from Earth in the constellation Aquarius. The star itself is only slightly larger than Jupiter, and because it's so small and dim, its seven confirmed planets all orbit closer to it than Mercury orbits our Sun, meaning the entire seven-planet system would fit comfortably inside Mercury's orbital path. All seven planets are approximately Earth-sized, and at least three, TRAPPIST-1e, f, and g, sit within the star's habitable zone.
TRAPPIST-1e stands out as one of the most promising candidates discovered so far. It is remarkably close to Earth in mass (about 77%), radius (about 91%), density (about 102%), and surface gravity (about 93%), giving it an Earth Similarity Index of 0.95, among the highest ever recorded for a known exoplanet. Scientists believe it may have a compact atmosphere and liquid water oceans, though this remains under active investigation, recent James Webb Space Telescope observations of the system's innermost planets, TRAPPIST-1b and c, found no detectable atmosphere at all, underscoring how much is still unknown about the outer planets like e.
The TRAPPIST-1 system itself is estimated to be around 7.6 billion years old, roughly 3 billion years older than our own solar system, meaning if life exists there, it would have had significantly more time to evolve than life on Earth has.
NASA's Exoplanet Travel Bureau has released a free downloadable poster imagining the view from the surface of TRAPPIST-1e, showing its six sister planets, some appearing far larger in the sky than our own Moon does from Earth. JWST has already dedicated more than 200 hours of observing time specifically to understanding the habitability of this system.
Source: NASA Exoplanet Exploration, TRAPPIST-1 System Overview. NASA Exoplanet Travel Bureau. James Webb Space Telescope, TRAPPIST-1 Observation Program.
#TRAPPIST1 #Exoplanet #NASA #TRAPPIST1e #HabitableZone

TjLzAtnA38g.description:
Proxima Centauri b sits 4.2 light-years from Earth, making it the closest known exoplanet to our solar system. And no telescope has ever directly photographed it.
Exoplanet detection almost never works by directly observing the planet itself, most are far too small and too close to their blinding host stars to image directly. Instead, astronomers rely on indirect methods, watching for what a planet's presence does to its star.
The most widely used method is the transit method. If a planet's orbit happens to carry it directly between its star and Earth, it blocks a tiny fraction of that star's light, causing a small, regular, repeating dip in brightness. This is how NASA's Kepler telescope found the majority of the thousands of exoplanets we know today. But a single dip isn't proof, scientists have to rule out other explanations, like stellar activity or a second star, before confirming a planet caused it.
Proxima Centauri b doesn't transit its star as seen from Earth, multiple dedicated searches have confirmed this. So it was found using a different method entirely, radial velocity. A planet's gravity doesn't just hold it in orbit, it also pulls back on its star, causing the star itself to wobble slightly around their shared center of mass. As the star wobbles toward Earth, its light shifts slightly blue. As it wobbles away, the light shifts slightly red. Astronomers measure this shifting to detect a planet they can never actually see.
In Proxima Centauri b's case, that wobble measured just 2 metres per second, roughly walking pace, in a star system 4.2 light-years away. The discovery was confirmed on August 24, 2016, in a peer-reviewed paper published in Nature by a team of 31 scientists led by Guillem Anglada-Escudé.
Scientists didn't need to see this planet to know it exists. They only needed to see its effect.
Source: Anglada-Escudé, G. et al. (2016). Nature, A Terrestrial Planet Candidate in a Temperate Orbit Around Proxima Centauri. NASA Exoplanet Exploration, Detection Methods. ESO, Pale Red Dot Project.

Elon Musk just open-sourced the actual algorithm behind X's For You feed. Now you can see why some posts fly and others don't.

Every post comes from two places: people you follow, and an ML system that surfaces people you don't. The model predicts what you'll do with a post, reply, repost, share, like or report, multiplies each probability by its weight, and sums it into one score that decides if it reaches you.

What stands out from the open weights: replies the author answers, reposts and link shares are worth the most, while a plain like sits near the bottom. An external link inside the post actually drags reach down. And one report hits a post like it lost almost 500 likes of reach.

The weights are public now, so this isn't guessing, it's straight from the code.

2VgKrwzmfBM.description:
Touching the Sun sounds impossible. It isn't, NASA's Parker Solar Probe has already flown directly through its corona, the Sun's outer atmosphere, becoming the first spacecraft to do so.

The Sun holds 99.8% of the entire solar system's mass. Every planet, moon, comet, asteroid, and particle of dust combined accounts for the remaining 0.2%. By volume, the Sun is large enough to hold approximately 1.3 million Earths.

Surface temperature averages around 5,500°C. At the core, temperatures reach roughly 15 million°C, hot enough to sustain thermonuclear fusion, where hydrogen atoms fuse into helium, releasing the energy that powers the entire solar system. The Sun is approximately 4.5 billion years old and is thought to be roughly halfway through its total lifespan. As it ages and its hydrogen fuel depletes, it will begin fusing helium into carbon, a transition that will cause it to expand into a red giant large enough to exceed Earth's current orbit.

One of the strangest unresolved questions in solar physics is the coronal heating problem. The Sun's visible surface, the photosphere, sits at around 5,500°C. Its outer atmosphere, the corona, reaches temperatures up to 200 times hotter, sometimes exceeding a million degrees. This defies basic thermodynamic intuition, temperature should decrease with distance from a heat source, not increase. First documented in 1939, the mechanism behind this remains actively debated among solar physicists, with leading theories pointing to magnetic wave activity and small-scale explosive events called nanoflares.

Despite its dominance over our solar system, the Sun is far from the largest star known. Stephenson 2-18, a red hypergiant located in the constellation Scutum, is estimated by some studies to have a volume roughly 10 billion times that of the Sun, though its exact size remains genuinely disputed among astronomers, with some analyses questioning whether it's even a confirmed member of the cluster used to estimate its distance.

Source: NASA Solar System Exploration, In Depth: Sun. NASA Parker Solar Probe Mission. Sky at Night Magazine, The Coronal Heating Problem. Simple English Wikipedia, Stephenson 2-18.

For the first time, scientists have demonstrated how AI can be used to design viruses that don't naturally exist, opening up a fascinating and potentially controversial new direction for biology.

The AI model involved is called Evo. Its architecture is inspired by the same general idea behind language models like ChatGPT, but instead of predicting the next word, it works with DNA sequences.

Evo was trained on approximately 9.3 trillion DNA letters from a wide range of biological sources, including bacteria, plants, animals, and microbes.

Researchers then used the model to generate new versions of a bacteriophage, a type of virus that specifically targets bacteria.

The scale of the experiment is what makes the story particularly interesting.

The researchers generated around 700,000 candidate sequences, selected a smaller group for laboratory testing, and found that 60 candidates produced replicating viruses.

Some of the resulting viruses also showed performance characteristics that compared favorably with the natural version.

So why does this matter?

One major problem facing medicine is antibiotic resistance. As bacteria evolve resistance to antibiotics, scientists are looking for alternative ways to target harmful bacteria.

That's where phages, or bacteriophages, become interesting. These viruses naturally infect bacteria, making them a potential tool for targeting bacterial infections.

But bacteria can evolve resistance to phages too.

The long-term idea is that AI could potentially help researchers explore and redesign phages much faster than traditional trial-and-error approaches, potentially creating new candidates as bacterial resistance evolves.

That doesn't mean AI has solved antibiotic resistance. There are still major scientific, safety, and regulatory challenges involved.

But the bigger shift is remarkable:

AI is moving beyond generating text and images. It's increasingly being used to design biological sequences and explore possibilities that scientists may not have discovered through traditional methods alone.

And that raises a much bigger question:

If AI can help design new biological systems, how far can this technology eventually go?

Andrew Ng has open-sourced OpenWorker, an AI coworker designed to go beyond the traditional chatbot experience.

Andrew Ng is one of the most well-known figures in AI. He co-founded Coursera, led Google Brain, and previously headed AI efforts at Baidu. So when he releases an open-source AI project, it's worth paying attention to.

Unlike a normal chatbot that simply responds to your prompts, OpenWorker is designed to take action across the tools you already use.

For example, you could ask it to prepare a customer brief, and instead of simply giving you instructions, it can create the document.

You can connect it to Slack, allowing it to work with messages and communication.

Connect your calendar, and it can interact with your events.

But one of the most interesting parts is that OpenWorker is designed to run locally on your Mac.

That means you can bring your own AI model and have much more control over where your data and workflows are processed.

It also includes an important safety mechanism: before taking certain consequential actions, the system can ask for your approval.

And this points toward a much bigger shift in AI.

We've gone from:

"Ask AI a question."

That's the difference between an AI chatbot and an AI coworker.

Claude’s AI watermark was supposed to make AI-generated content easier to identify. But the idea ran into a problem almost immediately.

In this video, we look at the growing challenge of identifying AI-generated content and why Claude’s watermark raises a much bigger question about the future of AI detection.

The basic idea behind an AI watermark is simple: if an AI system generates an image, video, audio file, or other piece of content, it can include an identifying signal that helps people or detection systems recognize that the content was created by AI.

That sounds useful.

But according to the story covered in this video, within roughly 48 hours of the watermark being introduced, a tool had already appeared that could remove it.

And that is where things get interesting.

If AI can generate content, another tool can remove the signal designed to identify that content, and AI detection systems themselves are not perfectly reliable, then the problem becomes much more complicated.

Now imagine the chain:

AI creates the content.

A tool removes the watermark.

Another system tries to detect whether the content was created by AI.

And the detector has to make a decision based on incomplete or altered signals.

This creates a potential cat-and-mouse game between AI generation, watermark removal, and AI detection.

The bigger issue is not really the watermark itself.

It is whether we can build a reliable way to establish the origin of digital content in a world where AI-generated media becomes increasingly realistic and increasingly easy to modify.

That matters for creators, businesses, journalists, educators, platforms, and everyday internet users.

Because as AI-generated content becomes normal, one question becomes increasingly difficult to answer:

Was this actually created by a human, or was AI involved somewhere along the way?

This video breaks down that problem, why AI detection is difficult, and what the future of identifying AI-generated content could look like.

Uploading PDFs directly into Claude could be using far more tokens than you realize.

A long PDF can contain a huge amount of text, formatting, charts, images, and other information. So even when you ask Claude one simple question, processing that entire document can become expensive in terms of token usage.

In this video, we show you a workflow that can potentially make working with PDFs in Claude much more efficient.

Instead of uploading the PDF directly, you can use Claude Code with a GitHub repository to convert the PDF into Markdown.

Markdown is essentially clean, structured text that can be easier for an LLM to process than a heavily formatted PDF.

But there is an important catch.

Markdown doesn't properly capture every visual element.

If your PDF contains charts, graphs, diagrams, screenshots, or important images, simply converting it to Markdown may lose information that Claude needs.

That's where Gemini comes in.

The workflow is:

PDF → Markdown → Gemini for visuals → Combine the outputs → Claude

First, convert the PDF into Markdown using the GitHub workflow.

Then, if the document contains important visuals, send the PDF to Gemini with the appropriate prompt so the visual information can also be extracted.

Finally, combine the Markdown content with the visual information and give the complete context to Claude.

The goal is to preserve the important information from the original PDF while potentially reducing unnecessary token usage.

This can be especially useful when you're working with long research papers, reports, business documents, technical PDFs, presentations, or documents containing lots of text and visuals.

Kepler-452b is a confirmed exoplanet detected by NASA's Kepler Space Telescope, announced in July 2015, located approximately 1,400 light-years away in the constellation Cygnus. Nicknamed "Earth's older cousin," it orbits a G2-type, sun-like star once every 384.8 days, just five percent longer than Earth's orbital period.

It is a super-Earth, roughly 60% larger in radius than our planet, with an estimated mass around five times Earth's, meaning surface gravity would be nearly double what we experience here.

Unlike our solar system, Kepler-452b appears to have no gas giant companion. For decades, the prevailing assumption was that a Jupiter-like planet is necessary to shield inner worlds from frequent asteroid impacts. Research by astronomers Jonathan Horner and Barrie Jones has challenged that assumption, suggesting a Jupiter-less system may actually experience fewer impacts, not more.

The more pressing concern is the age of its host star. Kepler-452 is approximately 6 billion years old, 1.5 billion years older than our Sun's 4.6 billion years, according to NASA's own announcement. As stars age, they grow larger, hotter, and more luminous. Kepler-452b may already be absorbing more radiation than its atmosphere can handle, potentially pushing it toward a runaway greenhouse effect, the same process believed to have transformed Venus from a possibly habitable world into the hellworld it is today.

Source: NASA, Kepler Mission Discovers Bigger, Older Cousin to Earth (2015). NASA Exoplanet Archive, Kepler-452b. Horner, J. and Jones, B.W. (2008), International Journal of Astrobiology.

I talk with Remy, known online as AI with Remy, about agent skills and how to share them across a whole team. Remy explains that a skill is an SOP for AI: a markdown file that teaches Claude your exact way to do a task. He then shows his system. He keeps his team skills in one GitHub repository, and he installs that repository as a plugin in Claude Code and Codex. The result is one source of truth, automatic updates for everyone, version control, and company ownership of the work. Listen to this episode if you run daily tasks with agents and you want your whole team to get the same quality of output.

Remy’s prompt + skill setup: https://startup-ideas-pod.link/Remy-skills

Timestamps

00:00 – Intro
02:33 – Skills as SOPs for AI
04:27 – How the agent uses skills
05:13 – AI is single player
06:21 – Example Skills: Notion, Brand Voice, Email
08:07 – How to share skills
11:40 – What is a Plugin?
14:58 – Anatomy of a Plugin
15:30 – Version Control and Rollback
16:58 – A Second Repo for Personal Skills
18:29 – The Day Claude Deleted 150 Skills
20:02 – Skills as Company Assets
21:00 – A Web App on Top of the Repo
24:46 – How Many Skills to Build
27:00 – The Self-Improvement Loop
28:15 – Skill Maxxing
30:40 – Closing Thoughts

Key Points

• A skill is a markdown SOP that teaches an agent your exact way to do a task.
• Most skills sit on one laptop, so a great process stays with one person.
• A GitHub repo plus a plugin gives the team one source of truth for every skill.
• Auto-update sends each skill edit to every teammate in Claude Code and Codex.
• A company-owned repo keeps the skills when a teammate moves on.
• Remy builds thin agents and thick skills, so any harness can run the same process.

Numbered Section Summaries

1. Skills as SOPs for AI 

Remy defines a skill as a markdown file that holds your full process, in the same way an SOP holds a process for an employee. He asks Claude for a sponsorship proposal, and Claude finds the proposal skill and produces a branded document in one shot. This matters because the model keeps your preferences from week to week.

2. The Microsoft Word Era of Skills 

Remy compares today's skills to documents in the early Microsoft Word years: each file lives on one machine, and copies spread by email. Google Docs solved that with one shared file. Skills wait for the same shift, and that gap is the theme of the episode.

3. Skills Worth Sharing 

He shows three skills from a single week: Notion formatting, AI with Remy brand voice, and email formatting for Resend. Each one captures a look and a standard that he wants across the whole team. Shared skills keep the output consistent, whoever runs the task.

4. Early Sharing Methods and Their Limits 

Remy walks through zip files on Slack, Google Drive, Dropbox, and Obsidian. Each method leaves duplicate copies, and Claude reads skills only from its own `.claude/skills` folder, so these setups need symlinks and manual repair. Technical teams cope with that; a junior marketer needs something simpler.

5. From Repo to Plugin 

The answer is a GitHub repo of team skills, grouped by department, installed as a plugin. In Claude Code you run `/plugin`, add the repo URL as a marketplace, and install the plugins you need. A few JSON files turn the repo into a plugin, and Remy had Claude write those for him.

6. Distribution, Updates, and Ownership 

With auto-update switched on, one edit reaches every teammate's Claude and Codex. Git history allows a rollback to any earlier version of a skill. The repo sits inside the company GitHub organization, so the business keeps the skills as an asset, and Enterprise accounts can push the plugin to everyone automatically.

7. A UI, a Skills Assistant, and Usage Data 

He built a web app that reads live from the team repo. It maps how skills call each other, such as a YouTube publish workflow that runs titles, thumbnails, and descriptions in sequence. An ask box recommends the right skill for a job, and a new hook counts each skill run per person, which shows the busy skills and the idle ones.

AI agents are the most trending topic in AI right now. And most people are too afraid to ask what they actually are. This video is the answer: what agents are, how they're different from just using ChatGPT or Claude, how the perceive-think-act-observe loop works, where agents go wrong, and how to start using one today for free.

Try your own AI agent free → https://instapilot.ai

Related videos:
→ Claude Cowork vs Manus: https://youtu.be/hmhr1_5TCK0
→ 10 AI trends changing everything: https://youtu.be/pMkMuejz9ZA

Stay up to date with all things AI with our daily newsletter → https://nocode.mba/newsletter?refer=youtube-video/Tkd8OuSyFss

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
WHAT YOU'LL LEARN:
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

1️⃣ CHATBOTS ANSWER, AGENTS ACT ChatGPT is one message in, one answer out. An agent completes tasks: it decides what to do, takes real actions, sees what happened, and keeps going until the job is done.

2️⃣ THE LOOP: PERCEIVE → THINK → ACT → OBSERVE The four-step cycle that repeats until the task is complete. How well it works depends on two things: the harness (the tooling and guardrails the agent works inside) and the quality of the model.

3️⃣ A REAL TASK, BROKEN DOWN "Find my last three invoices and email a summary to my accountant" — walked through step by step, showing exactly which integrations (file/email access) and tools (search, read, send) the agent needs at each stage.

4️⃣ CHATBOT VS WORKFLOW VS AGENT Workflows (Zapier, Make) are fixed pipelines that break when a step fails. Agents get a goal and tools, then choose their own path — and adapt when things go wrong. Sometimes a workflow is still the right answer.

5️⃣ REAL EXAMPLES My daily agent that researches whether Fable 5 is available again and emails me the answer, and a calendar agent that flags back-to-back meetings — all from a goal, not step-by-step instructions.

6️⃣ WHERE AGENTS GO WRONG Hallucinated steps (saying it sent an email it didn't), burning money on dead-end loops, and lacking judgment. The fix is the harness: deterministic code that verifies actions and stops runaway loops. Rule of thumb — don't give an agent tools you wouldn't let an intern use unsupervised.

7️⃣ WHY NOW? Three things converged: stronger models, cheaper inference (open models like GLM 5.2 near Opus quality for far less), and better tooling around agents.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
KEY TAKEAWAYS
 ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

💡 Chatbots answer questions; agents complete tasks — that's the whole distinction
💡 Goal + tools + freedom to choose the path = an agent
💡 The harness matters as much as the model — guardrails catch what agents get wrong
💡 Treat your agent like an intern: clear instructions, supervised tools
💡 A morning research brief emailed to you is the perfect first agent to try

💬 COMMENT BELOW: What's still confusing about agents? Tell me and I'll cover it in a future video.

China may be building an advantage in AI that has very little to do with AI models themselves.

In June 2026, researchers at the Institute of Plasma Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, completed testing on a 582-ton superconducting fusion magnet for China's “artificial sun” program. According to Chinese Academy of Sciences, the magnet is the world's largest fusion-reactor superconducting magnet, with three times the energy storage of ITER's comparable toroidal-field magnet and technology developed domestically.

That sounds like a fusion story.

But the bigger story could be electricity.

AI is becoming increasingly dependent on massive amounts of computing infrastructure, and computing infrastructure depends on electricity. The IEA estimates that global data-center electricity consumption could more than double from around 415 TWh in 2024 to roughly 945 TWh by 2030, with AI identified as the most important driver of that growth.

China is already seeing rapidly rising electricity demand from internet data services and AI-related infrastructure. At the same time, China is trying to connect computing capacity and energy infrastructure more closely together.

So the interesting question isn't simply whether China will achieve commercial fusion.

It's this:

If energy becomes one of the biggest constraints on AI, could control over abundant domestic energy become a strategic AI advantage?

Fusion is nowhere near being a guaranteed commercial power source yet, so this isn't a claim that China has already “won” the energy race.

But it highlights a much bigger shift in AI competition.

The next generation of AI competition may not only be about who has the best models or the most advanced chips.

Did you finally learn LangChain, LangGraph, OpenAI Agents, and all the other AI agent frameworks? You might want to pause for a second.

NVIDIA has introduced a research approach called NOOA, or NVIDIA Object-Oriented Agents, which takes a very different approach to building AI agents.

Instead of forcing developers to learn another specialized framework, the idea is to build an AI agent using familiar Python object-oriented programming concepts.

Think about an AI agent as a Python class.

Its methods can represent what the agent is capable of doing.

Its fields can represent the agent's state.

Its prompt can define how the agent behaves.

And type annotations can act as an enforced contract for what the agent should accept and return.

The interesting part is that this approach doesn't try to hide traditional software engineering behind another abstraction layer.

If you already understand Python and object-oriented programming, the mental model is much more familiar.

But there's an important caveat.

NOOA is still a research-stage approach, so it's far too early to say that it will replace frameworks like LangChain, LangGraph, OpenAI Agents, or Microsoft Agent Framework.

Still, NVIDIA's reported benchmark results make the approach worth watching, particularly around reasoning performance and token efficiency.

And that's the bigger lesson for AI engineers:

Don't get too attached to one framework.

The AI agent ecosystem is changing incredibly quickly. The framework you're learning today may not be the abstraction developers use tomorrow.

That's why keeping up with new research, papers, and open-source projects can be more valuable than simply mastering one framework.

Want the GitHub repository where you can keep track of new AI research and papers?

The biggest question, though, is how much access you’re willing to give an AI agent. Mario, the creator of Pi, shares the story behind his lightweight AI coding agent. Built out of a desire for control, minimalism, and determinism in software development, Pi offers a stark alternative to the complex, "token-maxing" tools coming out of Silicon Valley. 

At its core, Pi runs on a simple idea — a nested while-loop that sends a request to an LLM, handles whatever tool calls come back (bash commands, file reads, whatever the task needs), and keeps looping until it has an answer. No bloat, no black box. Built on Node.js/TypeScript across four core packages, it's designed so developers can actually read and understand the code their agent is writing. It even builds and extends itself, creating its own skills and extensions on the fly.

The film traces Mario's journey, from teaching himself to code on an Amiga 500 and QBasic in rural Austria, through the acquisition rollercoaster of RoboVM, to building Pi's open ecosystem today alongside co-founder Armin Ronacher. It's a story about what happens when you build software for control and clarity instead of chasing the biggest possible footprint, and why, in an industry obsessed with scale, "small and understandable" might be the more radical bet.

In this video, two AI agents run a full development cycle on a Microsoft Fabric data platform. The developer agent runs on Claude. It picks up a ticket from Azure DevOps, branches out to its own feature workspace, extends a metadata driven ingestion framework, tests the load against the source system, updates the project wiki, and opens a pull request. Then a reviewer agent running on OpenAI's Codex reviews that pull request before anything gets approved. The code gets written by one AI vendor and reviewed by a completely different one, so nobody is grading their own homework. My only job in the whole process is to write the ticket and press the merge button. And at one point, one of the agents catches a mistake that I made.

Both agents run under their own service principal identities, so nothing in this video runs as me. There is no human prompting them either: they get triggered by work appearing in Azure DevOps, they wake up on their own, and the only way I communicate with them is through tickets, comments, and pull requests. After the run I break down how the agents are actually built, and the patterns you can steal for your own platform: how to give agents a ready made toolbox so they don't burn tokens reinventing things, how to scope their permissions so autonomy is actually safe, and where the human has to stay in the loop.

Which AI workflows should I cover next? Leave a comment and let me know.

Topics covered:
- The platform: a metadata driven bronze ingestion framework, an Azure SQL source system, and an Azure DevOps project with a backlog, branch policies, and a wiki
- The project wiki as the agents' shared knowledge base: agents get onboarded like a new hire
- One ticket through the whole cycle: backlog, feature workspace, testing, documentation, pull request, review, merge
- The mistake beat: the agent's data quality check catches a wrong primary key in my ticket, and it stops to ask instead of improvising
- Cross vendor AI code review: Claude writes, Codex reviews
- The human merge gate: branch policy makes my vote the only one that can merge
- Agent anatomy: AGENTS.md, MCP servers, dispatchers, and service principal identities
- Guardrails: scoping permissions so the blast radius is capped before the agent ever runs
- Agents orchestrate, scripts execute: build the agent a toolbox first
- Why clean documentation and board history matter: agents read everything
- Where to start on your own platform: a PR review agent

#microsoftfabric #aiagents #dataengineering

About Sandustry

Sandustry is a factory automation game where every pixel is a resource waiting to be mined, mixed, processed, or destroyed. Explore a vast and fully-destructible open world as you seek out powerful artifacts left behind by an ancient civilization.

You’ve arrived on a vast unexplored planet filled with diverse biomes and beautiful landscapes – time to bring the fires of industry! From humble beginnings sifting gold from sand, you will quickly build a growing factory, unlocking powerful new technologies and production chains as you assess the viability of the planet for further industrialization. Countless options lie before you – will you focus on developing more advanced processing and logistical capabilities across your rapidly-expanding factory? Will you take advantage of local wildlife to aid with your mission? Or will you prioritize the hunt for artifacts, spending valuable resources to unlock access to their boons? And hey, there’s no faster way to mine than with the help of a rocket launcher, right? Build a beacon of industry and automation starting with nothing more than the trusty conveyor belt, incorporating filters, drones, pipes, pumps, and a myriad of other parts as you harness nature itself to do your bidding.

From individual grains of sand and flakes of snow to seeds, spores, and chips of ice, every pixel in Sandustry is a physical entity with its own properties. Discover countless chemical and physical reactions and exploit them to develop your production chains, building a pixel-perfect factory to optimize every step, or embracing chaotic webworks of conveyor belts and lifts as long as they get the job done – but be warned, sand is coarse, rough, and it gets everywhere, which introduces a new layer of complexity. The resources in Sandustry react to each other and the world around them – ice melts into water when heated, which turns to steam and rises if brought to a boil (only to come back down as rain if you let it reach the skies). Sand absorbs water around it, slowly depleting limited reservoirs, while stockpiles of slag can be burned and further processed to produce vital resources.

Deep beneath the planet’s surface lie countless mysteries for you to explore. Find clever ways to overcome the challenges left behind by an ancient civilization to uncover vaults of great knowledge and power. Nothing punches through a thick wall of ice like a freshly purchased flamethrower, but perhaps you can find a way to redirect some lava instead? 

Built with modding in mind, Sandustry lets you explore everything from visual tweaks and hand-crafted maps to entirely new buildings and processes that you can integrate into your production chains. Dedicated modding tools make it easy to customize your experience, share your ideas with the world, and even overhaul the whole game!

As you delve deeper into the planets of Sandustry and expand your industrial capabilities, the challenges will grow, but so too will your ways to overcome them. With fully destructible, procedurally generated worlds where every pixel is a resource to be harnessed, your options are limitless.

NVIDIA just released Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, an open AI model built specifically for fast, long-running agentic workloads, and it is now available inside Cline.

And this could make AI coding much more accessible to developers who want to run models locally.

Nemotron 3.5 Lightning is a 30-billion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model, but only around 3 billion parameters are active per forward pass. It supports a context window of up to 1 million tokens and is specifically designed for high-volume execution inside AI agents.

The interesting part is its speed.

NVIDIA reports that Lightning can deliver up to 4x the output speed of comparable models, making it particularly suited to agentic coding workflows where the model may need to make repeated calls, inspect files, run tests, fix errors, and continue working.

And Cline has already integrated it.

You can select Nemotron 3.5 Lightning in Cline through OpenRouter and start experimenting.

But there's an even bigger reason developers should pay attention.

NVIDIA is releasing the model as an open model, with weights, data, and training recipes available under its OpenMDW license. The model is also designed to be deployed locally or in the cloud.

Depending on your hardware, you can run it locally. NVIDIA's model card lists single-GPU deployment options including DGX Spark and H100, while the quantized version also supports hardware such as the RTX 5090.

That changes the economics of AI coding.

Instead of paying an API provider every time an agent makes another model call, developers can potentially run an open model on their own hardware.

But there's an important distinction:

Free model weights don't mean zero cost.

You still need suitable hardware, electricity, storage, and potentially additional infrastructure.

So this isn't necessarily about replacing Claude, Gemini, or OpenAI overnight.

The bigger story is that AI coding is becoming increasingly commoditized.

And NVIDIA, a company that makes enormous amounts of money selling the infrastructure AI companies need, is also pushing open models that let developers run AI closer to their own machines.

That's a fascinating shift in the AI ecosystem.

This is particularly interesting for people using coding agents such as Claude Code or Codex.

Give the AI a task.

Instead of giving it every individual instruction, the agent can determine the steps required to complete that task and interact with the computer along the way.

That could mean opening applications, navigating interfaces, running commands, working with files, testing software, and handling repetitive digital workflows.

And because the underlying project is open-source, developers can experiment with the technology and build their own workflows around it.

I sit down with Billy Howell for an inside look at a real business that runs on Grok Bot agent teams. Billy tests hundreds of tools for The Rundown, and he uses Grok Bot to run his local newsletter, The Arlington Bagel, which goes to 6,000 readers every Thursday. He walks me through his chief of staff bot, his research and sales agents, and the routines that move work forward while he sleeps. We cover the token math, the four-week plan he follows, and the business models that fit this tool best: newsletters, directories, and Shopify stores. You leave with a setup you can copy for one project this month.

Key Points

• Keep one project per Grok Bot account, so context stays clean and tokens stay available.
• Start with a chief of staff bot, and let it audit your business and name the first three agents.
• Follow the four weeks: build the team, execute, hire and fire, then automate.
• Ask each agent for a five-line brief: what shipped, what is stuck, what needs you.
• Move repeatable steps into scripts or make com, and keep agent tokens for high value work.
• Newsletters and directories give the easiest entry, and the two models feed each other.

Numbered Section Summaries

1. One Project, One Agent Team
Billy runs each Grokbot account on a single mission. Several businesses in one account cause context bloat, slow work, and heavy token use. He pays $200 a month for a second account that holds his Shopify experiment alone.

2. Design as a Feature
Grokbot gives you a limited set of agents, and Billy counts roughly 76 to 88 shape and color combinations. One thread per bot works like a direct message to a teammate, so he finds each agent fast and saves switching costs.

3. The Chief of Staff Audit
Billy picks a chief of staff first and connects it to Notion, Slack, and Gmail. On day one it takes stock of the business and names the top three agents that drive revenue. His audit produces a research agent, a sales agent, and a Beehive platform expert.

4. Build, Execute, Expand, Automate
Week one builds the team. Week two stays on execution alone. Week three fills the real gaps, such as an inbox agent. Week four adds routines, so the team moves the ball while Billy sleeps.

5. Routines and Five-Line Briefs
Each agent sends a short daily or weekly report to the chief of staff: what shipped, what is stuck, and what needs the human. Five lines keep tokens and context tight, and the chief of staff routes the rest of the work.

6. Teach Agents to Review Like You
Billy runs adversarial QA loops with a panel of subagents across three rounds, and output moves from about 50 percent done to about 90 percent done. He then turns a feedback thread into a skill, so another agent reviews work in his own style.

7. The Newsletter Machine
A research bot checks his source list twice a week and fills Notion cards with restaurant news and events. A make.com step formats each blurb the same way every week, and Beehive sends the issue on Thursday. His sales agent watches the Gmail inbox, prices the ad slots, builds a sales sheet, and found a local bagel shop sponsor this week.

8. Directories, Shopify, and the Site Builder Stack
Billy runs a stack of Cloudflare, Porkbun, Astro, and GitHub, and he shipped a live booking page from the beach in two or three hours. For directories, a research agent writes a brand page as markdown each day and a coding agent publishes it. He calls a newsletter plus a directory the lowest barrier entry point for a Grokbot business.

This visual architecture walkthrough explains the core production AI agent stack, from FastAPI and LangGraph to Postgres, Redis, model routing, observability, testing, and AI evaluations.

We begin with a local Python application that calls an LLM. Then, one responsibility at a time, we add the layers needed when real users, persistent data, changing model providers, failures, and quality requirements enter the picture.

My AI courses: https://edwarddonner.com/curriculum

--
Are we all becoming professional code reviewers? Students and companies keep asking me about the 'ADLC'... the evolution of the SDLC for the age of coding agents.

In this video, I try to bring clarity to what is still an evolving picture. I break down the ADLC into 3 parts:

1. The harness. How harness engineering is applied for your project, enforcing project standards and processes. Pre-commit hooks, repo as memory, CI/CD workflows.

2. The handoffs. The way we interface with the Agent. Still up for debate, but right now it seems Spec-As-Source is out and Spec-Anchored Intent is in.

3. The humans. A named person is accountable for every PR; approving the plan, confirming assumptions, checking success criteria. But reviewing every line of code? There’s an asymmetry: it’s far faster to generate code than review it.

I don’t have all the answers.
But I have some of them in this video.
And it will make a nice break from all those code reviews.
